newsitem.title: USA: Iditarod leaders start run up Bering Sea coast.
newsitem.headline: Iditarod leaders start run up Bering Sea coast.

text.p: Martin Buser, closing in on his third Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race championship, was the first competitor to reach the frozen Bering Sea coast Sunday and begin the final sprint to Nome.

Buser reached Unalakleet, an Inupiat Eskimo village 229 miles from the race's Nome finish line, at 7:54 a.m. (11:54 a.m. EST). He rested for five hours then was the first musher reported to have departed Unalakeet.
Buser was followed into Unalakleet about two hours later by Montana musher Doug Swingley, 1995 champion of the grueling 1,161-mile race from Anchorage.
Two other top mushers -- two-time champion Jeff King and perennial contender DeeDee Jonrowe -- arrived at Unalakleet within four hours of Swingley.
Despite a widening lead over Swingley, Buser said he was not taking a victory and its $50,000 prize for granted.
"It's too early to tell," he said in a radio interview broadcast from Unalakleet. "I hate being chased. It's horrible. That's why I try to get away from them."

Still, the Swiss-born musher said, it was better to be chased than to do the chasing in the final stretch of the world's most famous sled-dog race. "It's a more exhilarating feeling to be chased, but it's not a very comfortable feeling, either," said Buser, of Big Lake, Alaska.
King and Jonrowe, meanwhile, have stuggled with various ailments.
King, who won last year and in 1993, was stricken with illness midway in the race. The Denali, Alaska, musher has been battling his sickness with antibiotics.
Jonrowe has persevered despite severe injuries she suffered in a November auto crash. Her husband said the Willow, Alaska, musher had very little use of her left arm due to a rotator cuff tear.

The most debilitating effect, however, was the loss of training time, said Mike Jonrowe. Weeks of hospitalization and convalescence eroded her fitness level and robbed her of important practice time with the dogs, he said.
Fifty-three mushers began the Iditarod on March 1 in downtown Anchorage. As of Sunday, five had dropped out of the competition.
